A plaudit is an enthusiastic expression of praise or approval — a strong, open, and often public show of admiration for something someone has done. Think of it as praise that is loud in spirit, whether spoken out loud, written, or shown through applause.

When a brilliant scientist announces a groundbreaking discovery and the entire room bursts into cheering and clapping, those cheers and that applause are plaudits. When critics rave about a film and shower it with glowing reviews, those reviews are plaudits. When a crowd gives a performer a standing ovation, that ovation is a plaudit.

In short: a plaudit is praise with energy and enthusiasm behind it.
Singular vs. Plural — An Important Note

You will almost always see this word in its plural form: "plaudits." This is so common that some people go their whole lives reading and writing English without ever encountering the singular "plaudit." Both are correct, but "plaudits" is the natural, everyday form.

Think of it like the word "congratulations" — you wouldn't normally say "congratulation," and in the same way, "plaudits" flows far more naturally than "a plaudit."

So in real usage: "She received plaudits from the entire industry" sounds natural. "She received a plaudit from the entire industry" sounds slightly odd, though it is technically correct.
What Makes It Different from Just "Praise"

"Praise" is a broad, general word. You can praise a child quietly for tying their shoes. That is gentle, everyday praise.

Plaudits carry more weight. They suggest:

Enthusiasm — Plaudits are not mild or reluctant. There is real excitement and admiration behind them.

A sense of audience or community — Plaudits often come from a group of people, a crowd, critics, an industry, or the general public — not just one person whispering a compliment. They feel collective and public.

A noteworthy achievement — Plaudits are not given for ordinary things. They are earned by standout performances, remarkable work, or impressive deeds that genuinely move people to express their admiration loudly and openly.

So while any warm word of appreciation is "praise," plaudits are the kind of praise that sweeps through a room or across an entire field.
How It's Used in Real Life

Plaudits appear most naturally in formal writing, journalism, literary fiction, and thoughtful speech. You will see it in newspaper reviews, award coverage, speeches, and professional commentary. It is not a word you would casually drop in a text message to a friend — it lives in slightly elevated language.

Here are some natural example sentences to cement the feel of it:

  • "The director's latest film has earned widespread plaudits from critics across the world."
  • "Despite the plaudits she received after her speech, she remained modest and soft-spoken."
  • "The team's performance in the final drew plaudits even from rival fans."
  • "His novel was met with plaudits when it was first published, and it has only grown in reputation since."
  • "She worked hard for years without recognition, so when the plaudits finally came, they meant everything to her."

Notice the pattern: something impressive happens → people respond with open, enthusiastic admiration → that admiration is called "plaudits."

In most cases, plaudits are genuine. However, like many words for praise, "plaudits" can occasionally be used sarcastically to mean the opposite:

"Well, he'll certainly win no plaudits for that decision."

Here the speaker means the person deserves criticism, not praise. This sarcastic use is less common but worth knowing so it doesn't confuse you when you see it.
Close Synonyms and How Plaudit Differs from Each

Understanding a word is sharpened by knowing what sets it apart from its neighbors.

Praise is the widest, most general term. Plaudits are a specific, enthusiastic, often public kind of praise.

Acclaim is very close to plaudits in meaning — both suggest enthusiastic public approval. "Acclaim" is possibly even more intense and widespread ("worldwide acclaim"), while "plaudits" can be from a smaller but still enthusiastic group.

Accolade refers to a formal honor, award, or distinction — more structured and official. Plaudits are more spontaneous and expressive. You can win an accolade (a trophy, a title), but plaudits are the human reaction of admiration, not a physical reward.

Applause is the literal physical act of clapping. Plaudits can mean applause, but they also reach further to include any enthusiastic expression of approval — written, spoken, or shown.

Kudos is an informal word for credit and praise. Plaudits are more formal and carry a grander, more ceremonious feeling.

If you want one mental image to lock this word in your memory forever: picture a theater after a magnificent performance. The curtain falls. The entire audience rises to their feet, clapping, cheering, calling out in delight. That wave of joyful, open, collective admiration washing over the performer — that is the feeling "plaudits" captures. It is praise at its most alive, most visible, and most heartfelt.
